content: 1. Among the seven good practice statements, three are identical for both the general population of women and women living with HIV, while two are distinct and specific to each population. The recommendations and good practice statements are grouped into two columns: one for the general population of women (nos. 1–14) and another for women living with HIV (nos. 21–34). Additionally, there is a section where the populations are not separated. 2. Currently, there are 11 recommendations and three good practice statements for each population in the first grouping, with an additional recommendation and good practice statement applicable to both populations in the second grouping. The numbering has gaps because the WHO plans to issue additional recommendations soon, particularly on screening tests and implementation, which are expected to be numbered 15–20 for the general population and 35–40 for women living with HIV. 3. The WHO recommends using HPV DNA detection as the primary screening test instead of VIA or cytology in screening and treatment approaches for both the general population of women and women living with HIV. This is a strong recommendation based on moderate-certainty evidence. 4. In a screen-and-treat approach using HPV DNA detection as the primary screening test, the WHO suggests treating women who test positive for HPV DNA in the general population. This is a conditional recommendation with moderate-certainty evidence. 5. In a screen, triage, and treat approach using HPV DNA detection as the primary screening test among the general population, the WHO suggests using partial genotyping, colposcopy, VIA, or cytology to triage women after a positive HPV DNA test. The choice of triage method depends on feasibility, training, program quality assurance, and available resources in different countries. This is a conditional recommendation with moderate-certainty evidence. 6. For women living with HIV, the WHO also suggests using partial genotyping, colposcopy, VIA, or cytology to triage women after a positive HPV DNA test in a screen, triage, and treat approach. The benefits, harms, and programmatic costs of the triage options are similar, and the choice of method depends on local feasibility and resources. This is a conditional recommendation with moderate-certainty evidence. 7. The WHO suggests starting regular cervical cancer screening at the age of 25 years among women living with HIV. Evidence indicates that there are likely to be very few women living with HIV who develop cervical cancer before the age of 25. This is a conditional recommendation with low-certainty evidence. 8. After the age of 50 years, the WHO suggests stopping screening after two consecutive negative screening results consistent with the recommended regular screening intervals for both the general population of women and women living with HIV. VIA and ablative treatment are not suitable for women in whom the transformation zone is not visible. This is a conditional recommendation with low-certainty evidence. 9. Priority should be given to screening women aged 30–49 years in the general population. This is a good practice statement. 10. The WHO suggests a regular screening interval of every 5–10 years when using HPV DNA detection as the primary screening test among the general population of women. This is a conditional recommendation with low-certainty evidence. 11. For women living with HIV, the WHO suggests a regular screening interval of every 3–5 years when using HPV DNA detection as the primary screening test. This is a conditional recommendation with low-certainty evidence. 12. While transitioning to a program with a recommended regular screening interval, screening even just twice in a lifetime is beneficial for both the general population of women and women living with HIV. This is a good practice statement. 13. As programs introduce HPV DNA testing, this test should be used at the woman’s next routine screening date, regardless of the test used at prior screenings. In existing programs using cytology or VIA as the primary screening test, rescreening with the same test should continue until HPV DNA testing becomes operational. This is a good practice statement. 14. Once a decision to treat a woman is made—whether from the general population or women living with HIV—it is good practice to treat as soon as possible, ideally within six months, to reduce the risk of loss to follow-up. However, in pregnant women, treatment should be deferred until after pregnancy. This is a good practice statement. 15. The WHO suggests large-loop excision of the transformation zone (LLETZ) or cold knife conization (CKC) for women from both the general population and women living with HIV who have histologically confirmed adenocarcinoma in situ (AIS). Loop excision may be preferred in women of reproductive age, in settings with greater availability of LLETZ, and by providers with greater expertise in performing LLETZ. This is a conditional recommendation with low-certainty evidence. 16. Cervical cancer remains a leading cause of mortality among women. In 2020, an estimated 604,000 women were diagnosed with cervical cancer worldwide, and approximately 342,000 women died from the disease. It is the most commonly diagnosed cancer in 23 countries and the leading cause of cancer death in 36 countries, primarily in sub-Saharan Africa, Melanesia, South America, and South-Eastern Asia. 17. In May 2018, the WHO Director-General issued a call to action for the elimination of cervical cancer. The WHO global strategy to accelerate the elimination of cervical cancer as a public health problem was endorsed in August 2020. The targets for 2030 include vaccinating 90% of eligible girls against HPV, screening 70% of eligible women at least twice in their lifetimes, and effectively treating 90% of those with a positive screening test or cervical lesion, including palliative care when needed. 18. Cervical cancer prevention plays a critical role in achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly those related to health (SDG 3) and gender equality (SDG 5). 19. Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) is characterized by cellular changes in the transformation zone of the cervix, typically caused by high-risk HPV infections, particularly strains 16 and 18, which account for over 70% of cervical cancers. CIN1 lesions, also known as low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions, are morphological correlates of HPV infections. 20. The traditional method for cervical cancer screening has been cytology (Pap smear). Positive cytology results are confirmed by colposcopy, and treatment decisions are informed by biopsy and histological diagnosis of suspicious lesions.
